summary: Gives an overview of the MIKEY key management protocol, defined in RFC 3830, its four key distribution methods and the extensions made since. It explains use cases, motivations, and advantages so developers and architects can choose among modes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: MIKEY is a way to share secret keys for calls. This guide compares the different ways to hand over the key and when each is a good choice.

subtitle: Comparing the ways to hand off secret keys for encrypted calls.

tldr.problem: MIKEY, a key management protocol for secure real-time communication, defines several ways to distribute encryption keys, but choosing among them is complex because each has different trade-offs in scalability, performance, and security properties.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC surveys MIKEY's four original modes plus three extensions, describing the mechanisms, advantages and disadvantages of each, and when they apply to SIP call scenarios like early media, call forwarding, and conferencing.
tldr.outcome: Developers can use this guide to select the right key distribution method for their deployment; no single method is best for all cases.

facts.label: MIKEY packet round trips
facts.value: At most 1 (some modes need full round trip)

today: RFC 5197 is informational and provides guidance on MIKEY as of 2008. MIKEY itself (RFC 3830) is still in use, though newer protocols like DTLS-SRTP have emerged as alternatives for key establishment in WebRTC and other modern systems.

sections.title: Key Distribution Methods
sections.content:
MIKEY (Multimedia Internet KEYing), defined in RFC 3830, is a protocol that establishes cryptographic keys for SRTP (Secure Real-Time Transport Protocol) and other security protocols. It supports multiple key distribution methods, each suited to different scenarios.

The base RFC 3830 defines four methods: symmetric pre-shared keys (PSK), asymmetric keys (RSA), Diffie-Hellman key agreement with signatures (DHSIGN), and unprotected key distribution (NULL). Extensions add three more: DH with pre-shared keys (DHHMAC), SAML-assisted DH (DHSAML), and RSA with in-band certificates (RSA-R). This RFC explains each mode's trade-offs.
sections.eli5: MIKEY is a way to share a secret key between two people on a call. There are seven ways to do it, and some are faster, some are safer, some work better when servers are listening.

sections.title: The Base Modes
sections.content:
Pre-Shared Key (PSK) mode: Both parties know a secret in advance (out-of-band). The initiator sends key material encrypted with that secret; the responder verifies. Advantages: simple, low bandwidth, no PKI needed. Disadvantages: no forward secrecy, only the initiator generates the key, does not scale to large groups.

Public Key (RSA) mode: The initiator generates the key and sends it encrypted with the responder's public key. Advantages: no pre-shared secret, forward secrecy (somewhat). Disadvantages: requires the responder's certificate in advance, responder cannot influence the key, depends on PKI for verification.

Diffie-Hellman with Signatures (DHSIGN): Both parties contribute to the key using Diffie-Hellman; signatures authenticate the exchange. Advantages: mutual key agreement, perfect forward secrecy, self-signed certificates work. Disadvantages: requires PKI for scaling, point-to-point only, slower (full round trip).

Unprotected (NULL): Key is sent in plaintext, relying on the underlying layer (e.g., TLS) for security. Advantages: simple, no crypto overhead. Disadvantages: no message protection if TLS fails, no forward secrecy.
sections.eli5: PSK: you both know a password, encrypt with it. RSA: use their public key. DH: agree on a secret together. NULL: just send it in the clear, hope the network is safe.

sections.title: Extensions and Advanced Modes
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman with Pre-Shared Keys (DHHMAC): Combines DH for mutual agreement with HMAC authentication using a pre-shared key. Advantages: perfect forward secrecy, mutual key agreement, no PKI, works in trusted enterprise networks. Disadvantages: requires pre-shared secrets with each peer, useful mainly for small trusted groups.

SAML-Assisted DH (DHSAML): Uses SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) to pass signed Diffie-Hellman credentials from a central server. Advantages: mutual authentication, forward secrecy, supports group keying, reduces latency for credential validation. Disadvantages: two round trips, requires a server, opens risk of man-in-the-middle if the server is compromised.

RSA with In-Band Certificates (RSA-R): Similar to RSA, but the responder can send its certificate in the MIKEY message itself. Advantages: certificate does not need to be known in advance, efficient in multicast scenarios where one sender reaches many receivers. Disadvantages: no perfect forward secrecy.

Extensions also add elliptic curve algorithms (ECDH, ECDSA) for smaller key sizes and better performance on constrained devices.
sections.eli5: DH with shared key: both contribute, both must know a password. SAML: a server vouches for you. RSA-R: send your certificate along with the key.

sections.title: Choosing a Mode
sections.content:
The RFC discusses four SIP challenges. Early media (media before the SDP answer arrives) can create race conditions; PSK and NULL methods are simpler here because they do not require negotiation. Forking (a proxy splits a call to multiple destinations) can cause two-time pads if both branches get the same key and SSRC; RSA and RSA-R help because each branch gets a fresh key.

Call transfer and redirect risk sending a key to the wrong destination; SAML and DHSIGN reduce this by tying the key to the other party's identity. Shared key conferencing (a conference where all participants share one key) suits PSK and RSA modes but is complex with DH.

No single method wins all criteria. PSK is mandatory to implement (for backwards compatibility) but does not scale. DHSIGN provides strong security and forward secrecy but requires PKI and point-to-point communication. Architects must match the method to their trust model, performance needs, and deployment topology.
sections.eli5: If you want fast setup, PSK. If you care about forward secrecy and both sides contribute, use DH. If you are worried about the wrong person getting the key, use SAML.
